senses.gloss:
Bhūta-vidyā is one of the sciences enumerated in the Chāndogya upaniṣad. It seems to mean the ‘science of creatures’ that trouble men, and of the means of warding them off, ‘demonology.’
Foot notes vii. 1, 2. 4; 2, 1; 7, 1. Cf. Little, Grammatical Index, 115.

Bhūta-vīra is the name of a family of priests who, according to the aitareya brāhmaṇa, were employed by janamejaya to the exclusion of the Kaśyapas. A family of the latter, the Asitamṛgas, however, won back the favour of janamejaya, and ousted the Bhūtavīras.
Foot notes vii. 27. Cf. Roth, Zur Litteratur und Geschichte des Weda, 118; Eggeling, Sacred Books of the East, 43, 344, n. 3; Muir, Sanskrit Texts, 12, 437 et seq.

Bhūtāṃśa is in the Rigveda the name of a poet, a descendant of kaśyapa.
Foot notes x. 106, 11. See nirukta, xii, 41; Bṛhaddevatā. viii. 18. 19; Ludwig, Translation of the Rigveda, 3, 133.

Bhūti is the term used in the Rigveda and later for ‘prosperity.’
Foot notes viii. 59, 7. Cf. i. 161, 1 (both late passages).
Av. ix. 6, 45; x. 3, 17; 6, 9; xi. 7, 22; 8, 21; taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 1, 1, 1; 3, 5, etc.; bhūti-kāma, ‘desiring prosperity,’ taittirīya Saṃhitā, ii. 1, 1, 1; 2, 3, 3; v. 1, 9, 1, etc.
